questions.question_text: If $P(x) = 7x^{4} - 3x + 2$ and $Q(x) = 2x^{3} + 5x^{2} - 1$, what is the degree of $P(x)Q(x)$?

options.why: Multiplied the degrees $4 \times 3$ instead of adding them.
Took the maximum degree rather than adding the degrees for a product.
Multiplied the leading coefficients $7 \times 2$ instead of finding the power.

questions.question_text: What is the degree of the product $(3x^{2} - 1)(2x^{5} + 4x - 7)$?

options.why: Multiplied the exponents $2 \times 5$ instead of adding them.
Selected the highest exponent of a single factor instead of the product.
Multiplied the coefficients $3 \times 2$ rather than evaluating the degree.

questions.solution_text:
The leading term is $3x^{2} \times 2x^{5} = 6x^{7}$.
The degree is $2 + 5 = 7$.

questions.question_text: If $P(x) = 2x^{4} - 3x^{2} + x - 5$, what is the degree of $(P(x))^{3}$?

options.why: Added the power to the degree $4 + 3$ instead of multiplying $4 \times 3$.
Calculated $4^{3}$ instead of multiplying the degree by the exponent.
Assumed cubing the polynomial does not change its degree.

questions.question_text: If $P(x) = 4x^{3} - 2x + 7$ and $Q(x) = 3x^{5} + x^{2} - 6$, what is the degree of $P(x) + Q(x)$?

options.why: Added the degrees $3 + 5$ instead of taking the maximum degree.
Incorrectly multiplied the degrees $3 \times 5$; even for a polynomial product, the degrees are added.
Subtracted the degrees $5 - 3$ rather than taking the maximum.

questions.solution_text:
When adding polynomials with unequal degrees, the result takes the higher degree.
$\deg(P(x) + Q(x)) = \max(3, 5)$
$= 5$

options.why: Subtracted the highest exponents $6 - 4$ instead of taking the maximum.
Multiplied the exponents $6 \times 4$ instead of identifying the leading term.
Chose the degree of the second polynomial rather than the higher degree.

questions.solution_text:
The highest power of $x$ in the difference is $5x^{6}$.
The degree is $\max(6, 4) = 6$.

options.why: Assumed the sum retains degree $4$ without noticing that the $x^{4}$ terms cancel.
Selected the power of $3x^{2}$ instead of the surviving higher term $2x^{3}$.
Assumed every term cancels when only the leading terms cancel, and incorrectly assigned degree $0$ to the zero polynomial, which has no degree.

questions.solution_text:
Combining like terms:
$(6x^{4} - 6x^{4}) + 2x^{3} + 3x^{2} + x - 5 = 2x^{3} + 3x^{2} + x - 5$
The leading term is $2x^{3}$, so the degree is $3$.

questions.question_text: For what value of $a$ will the polynomial $(ax^{3} + 7x^{2} - 4) - (5x^{3} + 2x - 1)$ have a degree of $2$?

options.why: Failed to account for the subtraction sign in $(ax^{3} - 5x^{3})$.
Set the first coefficient to zero instead of cancelling with $-5x^{3}$.
Equated $a$ to the coefficient of the quadratic term.

questions.solution_text:
The coefficient of $x^{3}$ in the difference is $a - 5$.
For the degree to drop to $2$, the $x^{3}$ term must cancel:
$a - 5 = 0$
$a = 5$

questions.question_text:
$P(x) = (2x + 3)^{3}$ and $Q(x) = 8x^{3} + 36x^{2} + 50x - 1$.
What is the degree of $P(x) - Q(x)$?

options.why: Kept the original degree $3$ without checking cancellation of the cubic terms.
Checked cancellation of the cubic terms but missed that the quadratic terms also cancel.
Incorrectly cancelled $54x - 50x$, leaving only the constant term.

questions.solution_text:
$P(x) = 8x^{3} + 36x^{2} + 54x + 27$
$P(x) - Q(x) = (8x^{3} + 36x^{2} + 54x + 27) - (8x^{3} + 36x^{2} + 50x - 1)$
$= 4x + 28$
The cubic and quadratic terms cancel, so the degree is $1$.
